summary.text: Take \(n=7\). Since the prescribed \(x\) lies in \(\{3,4,6,10,15\}\), we have \(x\ge 3\); the ordering \(x\le y\le z\) then forces \(x+y+z\ge 9\), so no such triple can sum to \(7\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)\) count the positive integer triples
\[
0<x\le y\le z,\qquad x+y+z=n,
\]
for which all six integers
\[
2x-1,\quad 2y-1,\quad 2z-1,\quad 2xy-1,\quad 2xz-1,\quad 2yz-1
\]
are prime. The conjecture consists of the assertion that \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n>5\), together with the stronger assertion that whenever \(n>6\), one can choose such a triple with
\[
x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}.
\]

We disprove the strengthened assertion at \(n=7\).

Suppose, for contradiction, that the claimed representation existed for \(n=7\). Then there would be positive integers \(x,y,z\) satisfying
\[
x\le y\le z,\qquad x+y+z=7,
\]
and
\[
x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}.
\]
Every member of the displayed finite set is at least \(3\), so \(x\ge 3\). Since \(x\le y\), it follows that \(y\ge 3\); and since \(y\le z\), it follows that \(z\ge 3\). Consequently
\[
x+y+z\ge 3+3+3=9.
\]
This contradicts the required equality \(x+y+z=7\). Thus no ordered positive triple representing \(7\) can have its first coordinate in \(\{3,4,6,10,15\}\). This obstruction arises before any primality conditions need to be considered.

Because \(7>6\), the conjecture explicitly requires such a representation for \(n=7\). Its nonexistence therefore disproves the universal conjecture.

For completeness, this counterexample targets the “moreover” clause rather than the basic positivity claim. Indeed, \(7\) itself does have a triple counted by \(a(7)\), namely
\[
7=2+2+3.
\]
It is ordered as \(2\le2\le3\), and the six required numbers are
\[
2\cdot2-1=3,\quad 2\cdot2-1=3,\quad 2\cdot3-1=5,
\]
\[
2\cdot2\cdot2-1=7,\quad
2\cdot2\cdot3-1=11,\quad
2\cdot2\cdot3-1=11,
\]
all of which are prime. Hence \(a(7)>0\), but the valid least coordinate is \(2\), which is not in the prescribed set. The strengthened representation claim, and therefore the stated conjunction as a whole, is false.
